q: Find whether any two numbers in a SORTED array add up to a target. O(1) extra space.
why: Sorted plus pairs plus no extra space is the two-pointer signature. A hash map works too, but costs O(n) memory.
trap: A hash map works and is O(n) time, but it uses O(n) memory, which the prompt rules out.
depth: Duplicates like [3, 3] with target 6 still work because the pointers start at different indexes. Follow-up: what if the array isn't sorted?

q: Longest substring with at most K distinct characters.
why: Contiguous and 'longest' means a window that grows on the right and shrinks on the left when it breaks the rule.
trap: Binary search on the answer length can work, but it's slower and fiddlier. Contiguous plus "longest" is the window tell.
depth: Keep a count map and shrink from the left while it has more than K keys. Each index enters and leaves once: O(n). Follow-up: exactly K distinct = atMost(K) − atMost(K − 1).

q: Fewest moves to get from one cell to another in a grid with walls.
why: Unweighted shortest path is always BFS. DFS finds a path, not the shortest one.
trap: DFS finds a path, but not necessarily the shortest one.
depth: Mark a cell visited when you enqueue it, not when you pop it, or the queue fills with duplicates. If moves cost different amounts, switch to Dijkstra.

q: Keep track of the Kth largest number as new numbers stream in.
why: A min-heap holding the K biggest so far keeps the answer on top. Each insert is O(log K).
trap: Sorting after every insert is correct, but it's O(n log n) per new number.
depth: Push each number; if the heap grows past K, pop the smallest. The top is the Kth largest. Python's heapq is a min-heap, which is exactly what you want here.

q: Detect whether a linked list has a cycle, using O(1) memory.
why: Move one pointer 1 step and another 2 steps. If there's a loop, the fast one laps the slow one.
trap: A visited set works, but it costs O(n) memory.
depth: Follow-up: to find where the cycle starts, reset one pointer to the head and move both one step at a time. They meet at the entry.

q: Number of ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time.
why: ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2). Overlapping subproblems means DP. It's Fibonacci in disguise.
trap: Greedy (always take 2) counts one path, not the number of paths.
depth: You only need the last two values: a, b = b, a + b. n = 5 gives 8. Follow-up: allow steps of 1, 2 or 3.

q: Versions 1..n: once one is bad, all later ones are bad. Find the first bad version with few checks.
why: Good, good, good, bad, bad is a sorted yes/no sequence. Binary search for the boundary: O(log n).
trap: A linear scan is correct but can take n checks, and each check is the expensive API call.
depth: Use while lo < hi with hi = mid when mid is bad and lo = mid + 1 when it's good. The loop ends on the first bad version.

q: Group a list of words so anagrams end up together.
o: Hash map keyed by the sorted word
why: All anagrams sort to the same string, so that string is a perfect dictionary key.
trap: Two pointers compares one pair at a time; grouping needs a key that every anagram shares.
depth: Sorting each word costs O(k log k). A tuple of 26 letter counts as the key gets it to O(k).

q: For each day's temperature, how many days until a warmer one?
why: 'Next greater element' problems use a stack of items still waiting for their answer.
trap: A sliding window covers a fixed or contiguous range, but here each day waits a different amount.
depth: Keep indexes of days still waiting. While today is warmer than the top, pop it and record i − j. Each index is pushed and popped once: O(n).

q: Generate every subset of a set.
why: For each element you choose in or out, then recurse. That decision tree is backtracking. There are 2ⁿ answers, so no shortcut exists.
trap: Greedy makes one choice per element and produces a single subset.
depth: There are 2ⁿ subsets, so any method is at least O(n · 2ⁿ) once you count the output. With duplicates, sort first and skip equal neighbors at the same depth.

q: What does this print?
why: += on a list changes it in place, and x and y are the same list. Writing y = y + [4] would build a new list and leave x alone.
trap: Expecting [1, 2, 3] assumes y = x copied the list. It copied the reference.
depth: y = y + [4] would build a new list and leave x alone. This only bites with mutable objects like lists and dicts.

q: What does this print?
why: 'and' returns the first falsy value, or the last value if none are. 0 is falsy, so f(0) is 0. f(2) is 3.
trap: "False 3" assumes and returns a bool. It returns one of its operands.
depth: x or default uses the same rule and returns the first truthy value. It breaks when 0 or an empty string is a valid input.

q: What does this print?
code:
fs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in fs])
why: Each lambda looks up i when it's called, not when it's made. By then the loop is over and i is 2.
trap: [0, 1, 2] assumes each lambda captured i's value when it was made.
depth: Fix: lambda i=i: i binds the current value as a default argument.

q: What does this print?
code: print([i for i in range(5) if i % 2][::-1])
why: i % 2 is truthy for odd numbers, giving [1, 3]. Then [::-1] reverses it.
trap: [1, 3] forgets the [::-1] at the end.
depth: i % 2 is 1 for odd numbers, which is truthy, so the filter keeps the odds.

q: What does this print?
why: It peels off the last digit each call: 2 + 7 + 4 = 13. A digit-sum, the classic first recursion problem.
trap: 472 assumes the function rebuilds the number. It adds up the digits.
depth: Each call strips the last digit with n // 10 and adds n % 10. The recursion depth equals the number of digits.

q: What does this print?
code:
s = "berkeley"
print(s[1:4], s[-3:])
why: s[1:4] is indexes 1, 2, 3: 'erk'. s[-3:] is the last three: 'ley'.
trap: "erke" includes index 4, but the end of a slice is excluded.
depth: s[a:b] has b − a characters. s[-3:] counts from the end.

q: What does this print?
code:
a = (1, [2])
a[1].append(3)
print(a)
why: You can't reassign a tuple's slots, but the list inside it is still a normal mutable list.
trap: TypeError is what a[1] = [3] would give. Changing the list inside the tuple is allowed.
depth: That's also why this tuple isn't hashable: hash(a) raises TypeError because it contains a list.

q: What does this print?
why: Empty list is falsy. A list with anything in it, even 0, is truthy. And 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 in floating point.
trap: Calling [0] falsy confuses an empty list with a list that holds a falsy value.
depth: Compare floats with math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3).

q: What does this print?
why: make(1)(1) is 1 + 1 = 2. Then f(2) is 2 + 3 = 5. Each add remembers its own n.
trap: 4 forgets that f adds its own n, which is 3, to make(1)(1), which is 2.
depth: Each call to make creates a new add that remembers its own n. That's a closure.

q: What happens when this runs?
code:
def counter():
    n = 0
    def inc():
        n += 1
        return n
    return inc

c = counter()
print(c())
why: Assigning to n inside inc makes n local to inc, so n += 1 reads it before it exists. Add 'nonlocal n' to fix it.
trap: "Prints 1" assumes n += 1 updates the outer n. Assigning to n makes it local to inc.
depth: Add nonlocal n inside inc. For a module-level variable you'd need global instead.

q: This binary search sometimes never finishes. Why?
o: lo = mid should be lo = mid + 1
The loop should be while lo < hi
why: When lo and mid are the same index and a[mid] < t, lo = mid changes nothing and the loop spins forever.
trap: hi starting at len(a) - 1 is correct for this lo <= hi version.
depth: Trace a = [1, 3], t = 3: lo = 0, hi = 1, mid = 0, a[0] < 3, so lo = 0 again. It never moves.

q: This is meant to print [7]. What does it actually print?
why: Removing while looping shifts everything left, so the loop skips the next item. It removes 2, skips 4, removes 6. Loop over a copy instead.
trap: [7] is what you meant, not what runs. The loop skips the item right after each removal.
depth: Fix: nums = [x for x in nums if x % 2].

q: What's wrong with this graph search?
why: With any cycle in the graph it keeps re-adding the same nodes forever. Keep a visited set and skip nodes you've seen.
trap: popleft versus pop turns BFS into DFS, but neither causes the infinite loop.
depth: Add seen = {start} and only append nxt when it isn't in seen.

q: This 'memoized' Fibonacci is still painfully slow. Why?
o: It never saves results into memo
It recurses on the wrong values
why: It checks the memo but never writes to it. Store memo[n] before returning and it drops from exponential to O(n).
trap: The base case is fine: fib(0) is 0 and fib(1) is 1.
depth: Fix: memo[n] = fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2), then return memo[n]. Or put @functools.cache on the function.

q: Which input crashes this?
code:
def average(xs):
    return sum(xs) / len(xs)
why: An empty list has length 0, so you divide by zero. Interviewers love asking 'what about empty input?'
trap: [0] works: 0 / 1 is 0.
depth: Decide the contract first: return 0, return None or raise ValueError. Interviewers mostly want to see that you asked.

q: This should return the last k items. What's wrong?
code:
def last_k(xs, k):
    return xs[len(xs) - k - 1:]
why: Classic off-by-one. The slice should start at len(xs) - k. Simpler still: xs[-k:].
trap: k − 1 items would mean the slice starts one too late. It starts one too early.
depth: xs[-k:] is simplest, but watch k = 0: xs[-0:] is the whole list.

q: How many times does count += 1 run, as n grows?
why: The inner loop runs 0 + 1 + ... + (n-1) times in total, about n²/2. Constants drop, so O(n²).
trap: O(n log n) guesses the inner loop is cheap, but it averages n/2 steps.
depth: The total is n(n − 1)/2, which is 499,500 at n = 1,000.
title: How many times does count += 1 run, as n grows?

q: How many times does this loop run?
code:
while n > 1:
    n //= 2
why: Halving until you hit 1 takes log₂(n) steps. Any time you see halving, think log.
trap: O(n) assumes the loop moves one step at a time.
depth: n = 1,000,000 takes 19 halvings to reach 1.
title: How many times does this loop run?

q: a and b are lists of length n and m. Time complexity?
why: 'in' on a list scans the whole list. Turn b into a set first and the whole thing becomes O(n + m).
trap: O(n + m) is only true if b is a set.
depth: b_set = set(b) costs O(m) once, then each lookup is O(1) on average.

q: What does this duplicate check cost overall?
why: The sort is O(n log n) and the loop is only O(n). The bigger term wins.
trap: O(n) looks at the loop and forgets the sort before it.
depth: A set-based duplicate check is O(n) time, but it needs O(n) extra memory.
title: What does this duplicate check cost overall?

q: How fast does the number of calls grow?
why: Every call makes two more, so the call tree roughly doubles each level. Memoize it and it's O(n).
trap: O(n) is the memoized version, not this one.
depth: fib(40) makes over 300 million calls this way.
title: How fast does the number of calls grow?

q: Careful: how does this grow with n?
why: The inner loop always runs 10 times, no matter what n is. That's a constant. Nested loops aren't automatically n².
trap: O(n²) assumes every nested loop multiplies by n. This one multiplies by 10.
depth: Big-O drops constant factors, but 10n is still ten times the work of n.
title: Careful: how does this grow with n?

q: 8% of transactions are fraud. The model says "not fraud" every time. What does this print?
code:
y_true = [0] * 92 + [1] * 8
y_pred = [0] * 100
acc = sum(t == p for t, p in zip(y_true, y_pred)) / 100
print(acc)
why: 92% accuracy from a model that catches zero fraud. With imbalanced classes, accuracy mostly measures how common the majority class is. Look at recall, precision or PR-AUC instead.
trap: 0.08 is the fraud rate, not the accuracy. The model is right on every one of the 92 normal rows.
depth: Report a confusion matrix. With 8 positives, catching 6 is 75% recall, while accuracy barely moves.

q: Fraud model. A missed fraud costs $500. A false alarm costs a 2-minute manual check. Which metric do you push up first?
why: Misses are expensive and false alarms are cheap, so you want to catch as much fraud as possible: recall. Then pick the threshold where the extra review work is still worth it.
trap: Precision sounds safer, but it optimizes for not bothering people, which is the cheap side of this trade.
depth: Set the threshold by cost: flag a transaction when p × $500 is more than the cost of a review.

q: What does this print?
code:
tp, fp, fn = 30, 10, 20
precision = tp / (tp + fp)
recall = tp / (tp + fn)
print(precision, recall)
why: Precision: of the 40 you flagged, 30 were right, 0.75. Recall: of the 50 real positives, you caught 30, 0.6.
trap: Swapping them is the classic mistake. Precision divides by what you flagged; recall divides by what was really there.

q: What's wrong with this preprocessing?
code:
scaler = StandardScaler().fit(X)
X_train, X_test = train_test_split(scaler.transform(X))
o: The scaler saw the test rows, so test stats leak into training
StandardScaler can't transform the data it was fit on
why: Fitting on all of X uses the test set's mean and variance. Split first, fit the scaler on train only, then transform both. A Pipeline does this for you.
trap: It runs without errors, which is why this leak survives code review so often.
depth: Wrap it in Pipeline([('scale', StandardScaler()), ('model', LogisticRegression())]) and cross-validate the pipeline.

q: Predict next month's sales from 3 years of daily data. How do you split train and validation?
o: Train on earlier dates, validate on later ones
why: In production you predict the future from the past, so validation has to do the same. A random split lets the model peek at days that come after the ones it's tested on.
trap: Shuffled k-fold looks more rigorous, but it leaks future information on time series.
depth: Use walk-forward validation: train on months 1–24 and test on 25, then train on 1–25 and test on 26, and so on.

q: You're asked to predict ad clicks. What do you build first?
o: A simple baseline, like the average click rate or logistic regression
why: A baseline tells you whether the fancy model is worth anything. If logistic regression gets 95% of the lift, that's the answer interviewers want to hear you check.
trap: Jumping to the biggest model is the most common way to lose this question.
depth: Report the lift over the baseline, not just the absolute metric.

q: Your spam model scores 1,000 emails at 0.8. Only 500 of them are spam. What's the problem?
o: It's poorly calibrated: its scores overstate confidence
Nothing, scores are just for ranking
why: A calibrated 0.8 means about 80% of those emails are spam. Here it's 50%. Fix it with Platt scaling or isotonic regression on held-out data. It matters whenever someone uses the score as a probability, like setting a cost-based threshold.
trap: "Scores are just for ranking" is half true: ranking metrics like AUC can be fine while the probabilities are still wrong.
depth: Check it with a reliability diagram: bucket the scores, then plot predicted rate against observed rate.

q: Brute-force nearest neighbor: n stored embeddings, each of dimension d, one query. Cost?
why: You compute one d-dimensional distance per stored vector. That's why retrieval at scale uses approximate indexes like HNSW or IVF to avoid touching every vector.
trap: O(n) forgets that each comparison itself costs O(d).
depth: HNSW search is roughly logarithmic in n in practice, at the cost of a little recall.

q: What does this print?
code:
import math
a, b = [1, 0], [1, 1]
dot = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
cos = dot / (math.hypot(*a) * math.hypot(*b))
print(round(cos, 2))
why: dot = 1, |a| = 1, |b| = √2, so cos = 1/√2 ≈ 0.71. The vectors are 45° apart. This is the similarity score behind most embedding search.
trap: 1.41 is √2, the length of b, not the similarity.
depth: Normalize the vectors once and cosine similarity becomes a plain dot product.

q: Offline AUC went up, but the live A/B test shows no change in clicks. Best first thing to check?
o: Whether live features match the ones used in training
Whether the GPU is fast enough
Whether the model has more parameters
why: Training-serving skew is the usual culprit: a feature computed differently online, missing at serving time, or using information that isn't available yet. After that, check that the test had enough traffic to detect the lift.
trap: Model size feels relevant, but the offline gain already shows the model learned something; the question is why it didn't transfer.
depth: Log features at serving time and compare their distributions to the training data.

q: You're predicting which users will cancel. Which feature leaks the answer?
why: The cancellation survey only exists after someone cancels. At prediction time you'd never have it, so the model looks brilliant offline and useless live.
trap: Support tickets look suspicious, but they happen before the decision, so they're a legitimate signal.
depth: Ask of every feature: would I know this at the moment I make the prediction?

q: A spam filter's precision slowly drops over 3 months. Nobody touched the code. Most likely cause?
o: Data drift: spam changed, so inputs no longer look like training data
why: Spammers adapt. Monitor input and score distributions, alert on shifts, and retrain on recent data.
trap: Overfitting shows up right away on validation data, not as a slow decline in production.
depth: Data drift means the inputs changed. Concept drift means the link between inputs and label changed. They need different monitoring.

q: One request takes 40 ms of GPU time. A batch of 32 requests takes 120 ms. Average GPU time per request with batching?
why: 120 / 32 = 3.75 ms each, so throughput goes up about 10x. The catch: each request now waits for the batch to fill and run, so latency goes up. Batching trades latency for throughput.
trap: 120 ms is the batch's wall time, not the cost per request.
depth: Set a maximum wait, say 10 ms, so a half-full batch still runs. That caps the latency cost.

q: You downsample negatives 10x before training. What share of the training set is positive now?
code:
pos, neg = 80, 9920
neg_kept = neg // 10
print(round(pos / (pos + neg_kept), 3))
why: 80 / (80 + 992) ≈ 0.075, up from 0.008. The model will now predict probabilities about 10x too high, so correct for the sampling rate before treating outputs as probabilities.
trap: 0.008 is the original rate. Downsampling changes what the model thinks is normal.
depth: Correct it with p = q / (q + (1 − q) × 10), where q is the model's output and 10 is the downsampling factor.

q: This prints 0.99. Why isn't that good news yet?
code:
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(model.score(X_train, y_train))
o: It's scored on the training data, so it measures memorization
why: Any flexible model can ace data it has already seen. Score on a held-out validation set to learn how it will do on new data.
trap: The code is correct Python, so nothing errors. The bug is in what it measures.
depth: Use a held-out split or cross_val_score, and compare against a simple baseline.

q: 50 users have no referrer (NULL). What does this query return?
why: Comparing anything to NULL with = gives unknown, which WHERE treats as false. Use WHERE referrer IS NULL.
trap: It reads like it should be 50, and it runs without an error, which is what makes it dangerous.
depth: COUNT(referrer) also skips NULLs, so COUNT(*) − COUNT(referrer) counts the missing ones.

q: Why does this query fail?
code:
SELECT team, COUNT(*)
FROM players
WHERE COUNT(*) > 10
GROUP BY team;
o: Aggregates can't go in WHERE; use HAVING
GROUP BY must come before FROM
why: WHERE filters rows before grouping, so there's no count yet. HAVING filters the groups after: ... GROUP BY team HAVING COUNT(*) > 10.
trap: COUNT(*) is valid on its own; the problem is where it's used.
depth: WHERE and HAVING can both appear: WHERE filters rows first, HAVING filters the groups after.

q: Which loop does more work at n = 1,000?
why: A's inner loop grows with i, so it runs n(n − 1)/2 = 499,500 times. B always runs 20 inner steps: 20,000 calls. A does about 25 times more work.
trap: B looks heavier because 20 seems like a big constant, but A's inner loop keeps growing with n.
depth: At n = 10, B does more (200 calls vs 45). They tie at n = 41 and A pulls ahead after that. Big-O is about growth, not small inputs.

q: What does this print?
code:
grid = [[0] * 3] * 2
grid[0][0] = 9
print(grid)
why: * 2 copied the reference to one row, not the row itself. Both rows are the same list, so changing one changes both.
trap: The first option assumes * 2 built two separate rows. It built two names for one row.
depth: Fix: [[0] * 3 for _ in range(2)] creates a new row on each loop.

q: first_ge should return len(a) when every value is smaller than t. What does first_ge([1, 3, 5], 9) return?
why: hi starts at len(a) - 1, so the answer can never be len(a). Starting hi at len(a) fixes it.
trap: It doesn't loop: lo = mid + 1 and hi = mid always shrink the range.
depth: This is bisect.bisect_left. Test three boundaries every time: t smaller than everything, larger than everything, and equal to a value in the list.

q: A sensor sends millions of readings. At any moment you need the median so far. What do you keep?
o: Two heaps: a max-heap for the lower half, a min-heap for the upper half
why: Keep the two halves balanced, with sizes differing by at most one. The median is a heap top, or the average of both tops. Insert is O(log n), reading is O(1).
trap: One heap of size K tracks the Kth largest, not the middle, and the middle moves as data arrives.
depth: Python's heapq is a min-heap, so store negated values for the max-heap side.

q: is_valid_age(n) should accept 13 through 120, inclusive. Which test set is best?
why: Bugs cluster at edges, so test both sides of each boundary: 12 and 121 should fail, 13 and 120 should pass.
trap: 13, 50, 120 hits the edges but never checks that values just outside are rejected. That's where an off-by-one like n > 13 hides.
depth: This is boundary value analysis. If the function can receive other types, add inputs like "13" or None.

q: Each patient has 5 photos. You split photos randomly 80/20 and test accuracy is 97%. A new hospital gets 71%. Most likely cause?
o: Photos of the same patient landed in both train and test
The learning rate was too high
The test set was too big
why: The model partly learned to recognize patients, not the condition. Split by patient (GroupKFold) so nobody appears on both sides.
trap: More layers is tempting, but a bigger model would memorize patients even better.
depth: The new-hospital drop can also come from different cameras. Fix the group split first, then hold out a whole site to test for that.

q: Precision fell from 0.90 to 0.70 in a month. Input distributions look unchanged, but users report a new kind of spam. What's happening?
o: Concept drift: the link between inputs and label changed
A bug in the precision formula
why: Same-looking inputs, different meaning: the old features no longer separate the new spam. Get fresh labels for the new pattern and retrain.
trap: Data drift is the usual first guess, but the input distributions didn't move.
depth: Watching inputs alone can't catch concept drift. You need a steady trickle of fresh labels, even a small sample.

q: A reranker lifts search quality (NDCG@10) from 0.62 to 0.66 but adds 180 ms. You're at 90 ms today with a 200 ms budget. Ship it?
o: Not as is: 270 ms breaks the budget, so rerank fewer results or cache, then re-measure
Never, 180 ms is too slow for any search
Only if offline accuracy also improves
why: 90 + 180 = 270 ms, over budget. The usual fixes: rerank the top 20 instead of the top 100, use a smaller model, or cache popular queries. Then check the quality gain survives.
trap: "Quality always wins" ignores that slow results also lose users. The budget exists for a reason.
depth: Measure p95 latency, not the average. Then A/B test the cheaper version, because offline NDCG gains don't always show up as clicks.

q: 1% of people have a disease. Model A: 99.1% accuracy, finds 10 of 100 cases. Model B: 95% accuracy, finds 80 of 100. Which one screens patients?
o: B, it finds far more cases
A, fewer false alarms builds trust
why: Screening exists to find cases, and a follow-up test handles false alarms. A's accuracy comes from saying "healthy" to nearly everyone.
trap: Fewer false alarms sounds responsible, but missing 90 of 100 sick people is the costlier mistake.
depth: Out of 10,000 people, B flags about 560, so its precision is 80 / 560 ≈ 14%. That's normal for screening: a second test sorts out the alarms.

q: What does this print?
code:
nums = [4, 2, 7, 1, 8, 3]
best = s = sum(nums[:3])
for i in range(3, len(nums)):
    s += nums[i] - nums[i - 3]
    best = max(best, s)
print(best)
why: Windows: 4+2+7=13, then 2+7+1=10, 7+1+8=16, 1+8+3=12. Each step adds the new number and drops the one leaving, so the best is 16.
trap: 13 is only the first window. The loop keeps sliding and finds a bigger one.
depth: This works because the window size is fixed. If you want the shortest window with sum ≥ k, negative numbers break the shrink-when-too-big rule, and you need prefix sums with a monotonic deque instead.

q: What does this print?
why: At 3, 8, 5 nobody needed is seen yet (6, 1, 4). At 1 the code needs 8, which it saw at index 1, so it prints 1 3.
trap: 3 + 5 is 8, not 9. Check the sum, not just that both numbers look familiar.
depth: Checking before storing matters: storing first would let x pair with itself when target is 2·x. One pass, O(n) time, O(n) memory.
